newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Western economy undergoing dramatic change.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Western economy undergoing dramatic change.

text.p: The economy of the U.S. West is undergoing a dramatic change as such industries as entertainment, recreation and high-technology take on a more prominent role, according to a study released Monday by the Center for the New West, a Denver-based think tank.
The transition means the Western states are becoming less dependent on natural resources and moving beyond the boom and bust cycles that have characterized the history of the region, the center said.
The study, based on a consensus of economists from 11 Western states who met in June, also found that the economy of the Western United States will grow faster than the U.S. econony.

"Our national economy will be the premier economy in the industrial world, but the West will continue to grow faster than the national economy," said Thayne Robson, director of the Bureau of Economy & Business Research at the University of Utah.
Eight of the nation's top 10 job-producing states are in the West, led by Nevada, Utah and Idaho.
In December 1995, high-tech employment in Oregon exceeded the number of jobs in the forest products industry, traditionally that state's top employer.

In the same month in California, the last of the 500,000 jobs lost in the early 1990s, many in defense and aerospace, were replaced by new jobs in entertainment, multimedia, computers and other creative, information-based industries, the report said.

Even the traditional industries are taking on a new face, the report noted. In New Mexico, where jobs at military bases are being cut, the German Air Force is moving its entire training operation and more than 2,000 people to Holloman Air Force Base near Alamogordo to take advantage of modern facilities and clear skies.

But the growth is not without cost. Phoenix, Arizona, failed to meet Environmental Protection Agency clean air requirements, Utah faces a shortfall to pay for a needed highway construction project and even in Las Vegas anti-growth sentiments are on the rise, the report said.
